claim: IGF2 is an important mitogen in heart development.
source: We found that IGF2, an important mitogen in heart development, is required for neonatal heart regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about IGF2's role in heart development.

claim: IGF2 is required for neonatal heart regeneration.
source: We found that IGF2, an important mitogen in heart development, is required for neonatal heart regeneration.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: IGF2 originates from the endocardium/endothelium during neonatal heart regeneration.
source: IGF2 originates from the endocardium/endothelium and is transduced in cardiomyocytes by the insulin receptor.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by genetic lineage tracing experiments.

claim: IGF2 is transduced in cardiomyocytes by the insulin receptor during neonatal heart regeneration.
source: IGF2 originates from the endocardium/endothelium and is transduced in cardiomyocytes by the insulin receptor.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by genetic and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Absence of IGF2 abolished injury-induced cell cycle entry during the early part of the first postnatal week.
source: Following injury on postnatal day 1, absence of IGF2 abolished injury-induced cell cycle entry during the early part of the first postnatal week.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by pH3 staining data at 3dpr.

claim: Regeneration failed in IGF2-deficient neonates despite the later presence of additional cell cycle-inducing activities 7 days following injury.
source: Consequently, regeneration failed despite the later presence of additional cell cycle-inducing activities 7 days following injury.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by histological and pH3 staining data.

claim: Most cardiomyocytes transition from mononuclear diploid to polyploid during the first postnatal week.
source: Most cardiomyocytes transition from mononuclear diploid to polyploid during the first postnatal week.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ploidy analysis data in the manuscript.

claim: Regeneration was rescued in Igf2-deficient neonates in three different contexts that elevate the percentage of mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes beyond postnatal day 7.
source: Regeneration was rescued in Igf2-deficient neonates in three different contexts that elevate the percentage of mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes beyond postnatal day 7.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data from hypoxia, mCAT, and A/J strain experiments.

claim: IGF2 is a paracrine-acting mitogen for heart regeneration during the early postnatal period.
source: Thus, IGF2 is a paracrine-acting mitogen for heart regeneration during the early postnatal period, and IGF2-deficiency unmasks the dependence of this process on proliferation-competent mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by genetic lineage tracing and receptor activation data.

claim: IGF2-deficiency unmasks the dependence of neonatal heart regeneration on proliferation-competent mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes.
source: Thus, IGF2 is a paracrine-acting mitogen for heart regeneration during the early postnatal period, and IGF2-deficiency unmasks the dependence of this process on proliferation-competent mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by rescue experiments.

claim: Essentially all new cardiomyocytes after early embryonic development are generated by proliferation of preexisting cardiomyocytes rather than by differentiation from a non-cardiomyocyte progenitor source.
source: Once this early process has completed, in every later context in the embryo and throughout postnatal life, essentially all new cardiomyocytes are generated by proliferation of preexisting cardiomyocytes rather than by differentiation from a non-cardiomyocyte progenitor source (Sereti et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The rate of embryonic cardiomyocyte proliferation is high as growth of the heart keeps pace with overall embryo growth, but then tapers down by the end of gestation.
source: In mammals, the rate of embryonic cardiomyocyte proliferation is high as growth of the heart keeps pace with overall embryo growth, but then tapers down by the end of gestation (Soonpaa et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cardiomyocyte proliferation is minimal in normal heart biology for the remainder of life after gestation.
source: In normal heart biology, cardiomyocyte proliferation is minimal for the remainder of life; the heart grows considerably in size postnatally, but this is by the hypertrophic enlargement of existing cardiomyocytes rather than by generation of new cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about postnatal heart growth.

claim: The heart grows considerably in size postnatally by the hypertrophic enlargement of existing cardiomyocytes rather than by generation of new cardiomyocytes.
source: In normal heart biology, cardiomyocyte proliferation is minimal for the remainder of life; the heart grows considerably in size postnatally, but this is by the hypertrophic enlargement of existing cardiomyocytes rather than by generation of new cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about postnatal heart growth.

claim: The mammalian heart at late fetal and very early neonatal stages retains the ability to activate robust cardiomyocyte proliferation and to restore normal cardiomyocyte number in the context of an insufficient number of cardiomyocytes.
source: Nonetheless, in the context of an insufficient number of cardiomyocytes, the mammalian heart at late fetal and very early neonatal stages retains the ability to activate robust cardiomyocyte proliferation and to restore normal cardiomyocyte number.
evidence: This statement is supported by subsequent citations to prior work.

claim: Reactivation of cardiomyocyte proliferation to achieve efficient restoration of heart morphology has been observed in mouse genetic models that cause a non-lethal late-embryonic deficiency of cardiomyocytes.
source: Although there have been some negative observations (Andersen et al., 2016), reactivation of cardiomyocyte proliferation to achieve efficient restoration of heart morphology has been observed in mouse genetic models that cause a non-lethal late-embryonic deficiency of cardiomyocytes (Drenckhahn et al., 2008; Vincentz et al., 2017), and in surgical or congenital injury models that cause a neonatal loss of ventricular myocardium in rats (Robledo, 1956), mice (Sadek et al., 2014), and swine (Mahmoud and Porrello, 2018), and likely also occurs in human (Haubner et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Reactivation of cardiomyocyte proliferation to achieve efficient restoration of heart morphology has been observed in surgical or congenital injury models that cause a neonatal loss of ventricular myocardium in rats, mice, and swine.
source: Although there have been some negative observations (Andersen et al., 2016), reactivation of cardiomyocyte proliferation to achieve efficient restoration of heart morphology has been observed in mouse genetic models that cause a non-lethal late-embryonic deficiency of cardiomyocytes (Drenckhahn et al., 2008; Vincentz et al., 2017), and in surgical or congenital injury models that cause a neonatal loss of ventricular myocardium in rats (Robledo, 1956), mice (Sadek et al., 2014), and swine (Mahmoud and Porrello, 2018), and likely also occurs in human (Haubner et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neonatal heart regeneration likely occurs in humans.
source: Although there have been some negative observations (Andersen et al., 2016), reactivation of cardiomyocyte proliferation to achieve efficient restoration of heart morphology has been observed in mouse genetic models that cause a non-lethal late-embryonic deficiency of cardiomyocytes (Drenckhahn et al., 2008; Vincentz et al., 2017), and in surgical or congenital injury models that cause a neonatal loss of ventricular myocardium in rats (Robledo, 1956), mice (Sadek et al., 2014), and swine (Mahmoud and Porrello, 2018), and likely also occurs in human (Haubner et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work and is presented as likely rather than definitive.

claim: In mice, the plasticity to reactivate efficient cardiomyocyte proliferation is mostly lost by postnatal day P7.
source: In mice, the plasticity to reactivate efficient cardiomyocyte proliferation is mostly lost by postnatal day P7 (Porrello et al., 2011; Alkass et al., 2015), which is understood to mean that most ventricular cardiomyocytes have become postmitotic by this time.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Most ventricular cardiomyocytes have become postmitotic by postnatal day P7 in mice.
source: In mice, the plasticity to reactivate efficient cardiomyocyte proliferation is mostly lost by postnatal day P7 (Porrello et al., 2011; Alkass et al., 2015), which is understood to mean that most ventricular cardiomyocytes have become postmitotic by this time.
evidence: This is presented as an interpretation of the cited prior work.

claim: Heart injury in P7 pups or at any later time through adulthood is followed by insufficient cardiomyocyte proliferation and insufficient replacement of lost myocardium.
source: Consequently, heart injury in P7 pups or at any later time through adulthood is followed by insufficient cardiomyocyte proliferation and insufficient replacement of lost myocardium, i.e., by a failure to fully regenerate.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about heart regeneration capacity.

claim: Failure of regeneration after ventricular injury leads to a permanent diminishment of contractile function with possible further progression to heart failure in animals and humans.
source: In animals and humans, failure of regeneration after ventricular injury leads to a permanent diminishment of contractile function with possible further progression to heart failure.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the consequences of failed heart regeneration.

claim: Total DNA content may determine (rather than correlate with) proliferative ability of ventricular cardiomyocytes.
source: A number of differences distinguish ventricular cardiomyocytes at the beginning and end of the first postnatal week, but one that may determine (rather than correlate with) proliferative ability is their total DNA content (Gan et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work and is presented as a hypothesis.

claim: Essentially all fetal and early neonatal cardiomyocytes in mice have one diploid nucleus.
source: In mice and perhaps most mammals, essentially all fetal and early neonatal cardiomyocytes have one diploid nucleus (as is the case for most cells).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cardiomyocyte ploidy.

claim: During the first postnatal week in mice, cardiomyocytes undergo a last round of DNA replication followed by cell cycle arrest either before or after karyokinesis but without cytokinesis, resulting in mononuclear polyploid or multinuclear cardiomyocytes.
source: During the first postnatal week (in mice), cardiomyocytes undergo a last round of DNA replication followed by cell cycle arrest either before or after karyokinesis but without cytokinesis, resulting in mononuclear polyploid or multinuclear cardiomyocytes (Soonpaa et al., 1996; Alkass et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Only a few percent of ventricular cardiomyocytes after the first postnatal week and through the remainder of life are mononuclear diploid.
source: Typically, only a few percent of ventricular cardiomyocytes thereafter and through the remainder of life are mononuclear diploid, which correlates with the very low level of cellular and functional regeneration usually seen after adult heart injury.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cardiomyocyte ploidy.

claim: The low percentage of mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes correlates with the very low level of cellular and functional regeneration usually seen after adult heart injury.
source: Typically, only a few percent of ventricular cardiomyocytes thereafter and through the remainder of life are mononuclear diploid, which correlates with the very low level of cellular and functional regeneration usually seen after adult heart injury.
evidence: This is stated as an observed correlation.

claim: Adult zebrafish retain a very high percentage of mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes throughout adulthood.
source: Adult zebrafish retain a very high percentage of mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes throughout adulthood (Patterson et al., 2017; González-Rosa et al., 2018), and heart regeneration is robust in this species (Foglia and Poss, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Heart regeneration is robust in adult zebrafish.
source: Adult zebrafish retain a very high percentage of mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes throughout adulthood (Patterson et al., 2017; González-Rosa et al., 2018), and heart regeneration is robust in this species (Foglia and Poss, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: There is a precise correlation between the abundance of mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes and competence to support cardiomyocyte proliferation for embryonic heart growth or post-injury heart regeneration across multiple species and life stages.
source: Thus, from a comparison of multiple species and life stages, there is a precise correlation between the abundance of mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes and competence to support cardiomyocyte proliferation for embryonic heart growth or post-injury heart regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from comparative analysis.

claim: Polyploid cardiomyocytes are compromised in proliferation and regeneration in both mouse and zebrafish.
source: Recent experimental results in both mouse and zebrafish explicitly demonstrated that polyploid cardiomyocytes are compromised in proliferation and regeneration, and thereby confirmed the relationship between mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes and adult heart regeneration (Patterson et al., 2017; González-Rosa et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Some inbred mouse strains have a much higher percentage of adult ventricular mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes than others (e.g., 10% in strain A/J, compared to 2% in C57BL/6J).
source: Of particular relevance to this paper, we showed (Patterson et al., 2017) that some inbred mouse strains have a much higher percentage of adult ventricular mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes (e.g., 10% in strain A/J, compared to 2% in C57BL/6J), and that such strains have a correspondingly higher degree of both cellular and functional regeneration after adult heart injury.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Mouse strains with a higher percentage of adult ventricular mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes have a correspondingly higher degree of both cellular and functional regeneration after adult heart injury.
source: Of particular relevance to this paper, we showed (Patterson et al., 2017) that some inbred mouse strains have a much higher percentage of adult ventricular mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes (e.g., 10% in strain A/J, compared to 2% in C57BL/6J), and that such strains have a correspondingly higher degree of both cellular and functional regeneration after adult heart injury.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Organ regeneration following injury or tissue loss is generally thought to recapitulate at least some features of embryonic growth, including the redeployment of signaling pathways that had been active earlier in fetal development.
source: Organ regeneration following injury or tissue loss is generally thought to recapitulate at least some features of embryonic growth, including the redeployment of signaling pathways that had been active earlier in fetal development.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the field.

claim: The early embryonic heart consists of cardiomyocytes surrounding an inner layer of endocardium.
source: The early embryonic heart consists of cardiomyocytes surrounding an inner layer of endocardium (the endothelial lining of the heart).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about heart anatomy.

claim: Around embryonic day E10 in mouse, the epicardium migrates from a nearby source onto the outer heart surface.
source: Around embryonic day E10 in mouse, the epicardium, the noncontractile mesothelium of the heart, migrates from a nearby source onto the outer heart surface.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about heart development.

claim: The epicardium is the source of secreted mitogenic factors that promote cardiomyocyte proliferation in the embryonic heart.
source: In our past work, we showed that the epicardium is the source of secreted mitogenic factors that promote cardiomyocyte proliferation (Chen et al., 2002), and then identified IGF2 (insulin-like growth factor 2) as the major epicardial mitogen responsible for this activity (Li et al., 2011; Shen et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: IGF2 is the major epicardial mitogen responsible for promoting cardiomyocyte proliferation in the embryonic heart.
source: In our past work, we showed that the epicardium is the source of secreted mitogenic factors that promote cardiomyocyte proliferation (Chen et al., 2002), and then identified IGF2 (insulin-like growth factor 2) as the major epicardial mitogen responsible for this activity (Li et al., 2011; Shen et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Igf2 is expressed in the embryonic epicardium and endocardium but not myocardium.
source: Igf2 is expressed in the embryonic epicardium and endocardium (but not myocardium).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Mouse embryos deficient in Igf2 expression in all heart mesoderm or specifically in the epicardium lineage were substantially compromised in cardiomyocyte proliferation during the E10-E13 period.
source: Mouse embryos deficient in Igf2 expression in all heart mesoderm or specifically in the epicardium lineage were substantially compromised in cardiomyocyte proliferation during the E10-E13 period, which was morphologically manifest in a hypoplastic ventricle.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Conditional Igf2 mutation in the endocardium and endothelium had no phenotypic consequence in the embryonic heart.
source: Notably for the present study, conditional Igf2 mutation in the endocardium and endothelium had no phenotypic consequence in the embryonic heart (Shen et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Embryos lacking the two signaling-competent IGF2 receptors INSR and IGF1R in heart mesoderm or specifically in cardiomyocytes were compromised in cardiomyocyte proliferation and ventricular morphology.
source: Embryos lacking the two signaling-competent IGF2 receptors INSR (insulin receptor) and IGF1R (insulin-like growth factor one receptor) in heart mesoderm or specifically in cardiomyocytes were also compromised in cardiomyocyte proliferation and ventricular morphology (Li et al., 2011), which is predominantly a reflection of the importance of IGF1R rather than INSR in the embryonic heart (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: The embryonic heart phenotype of IGF receptor mutants is predominantly a reflection of the importance of IGF1R rather than INSR.
source: Embryos lacking the two signaling-competent IGF2 receptors INSR (insulin receptor) and IGF1R (insulin-like growth factor one receptor) in heart mesoderm or specifically in cardiomyocytes were also compromised in cardiomyocyte proliferation and ventricular morphology (Li et al., 2011), which is predominantly a reflection of the importance of IGF1R rather than INSR in the embryonic heart (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The midgestation hypoplastic ventricular phenotypes of conditional Igf2 or IGF receptor mutants were not so severe as to cause embryo lethality.
source: Although the midgestation hypoplastic ventricular phenotypes of conditional Igf2 or IGF receptor mutants were obvious, these were not so severe as to cause embryo lethality.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Cardiomyocyte proliferation in Igf2 mutants recovered to normal levels at E14.
source: Cardiomyocyte proliferation in mutants then recovered to normal levels at E14 (Li et al., 2011), likely in response to other factors distributed by coronary circulation that begins at that time (Cavallero et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: The recovery of cardiomyocyte proliferation at E14 in Igf2 mutants is likely in response to other factors distributed by coronary circulation that begins at that time.
source: Cardiomyocyte proliferation in mutants then recovered to normal levels at E14 (Li et al., 2011), likely in response to other factors distributed by coronary circulation that begins at that time (Cavallero et al., 2015).
evidence: This is presented as a likely explanation supported by a citation.

claim: Conditional Igf2 mutant pups were born in normal numbers and of normal size and health.
source: Mutant pups were born in normal numbers and of normal size and health, and conditional Igf2 mutants are viable and appear normal throughout a normal lifespan.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from prior work by the authors.

claim: Conditional Igf2 mutants are viable and appear normal throughout a normal lifespan.
source: Mutant pups were born in normal numbers and of normal size and health, and conditional Igf2 mutants are viable and appear normal throughout a normal lifespan.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from prior work by the authors.

claim: The other factors that restore cardiomyocyte proliferation in late gestation in Igf2 mutants seemingly do not signal through IGF1R or INSR and thus are not likely to be IGF1 or insulin.
source: Because conditional Igf1r/Insr mutants are also normal at birth, the other factors that restore cardiomyocyte proliferation in late gestation in Igf2 mutants seemingly do not signal through IGF1R or INSR and thus are not likely to be IGF1 or insulin.
evidence: This is presented as an inference based on genetic data.

claim: Igf2 mRNA is expressed in the epicardium and endocardium, although not in the myocardium, in the embryonic heart.
source: In the embryonic heart, Igf2 mRNA is expressed in the epicardium and endocardium, although not in the myocardium (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Only epicardial Igf2 has a required role in heart development.
source: As noted above, genetic analysis demonstrated that only epicardial Igf2 has a required role in heart development.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior genetic analysis cited earlier in the manuscript.

claim: The same expression pattern of Igf2 (epicardium and endocardium, not myocardium) persists into the early postnatal period.
source: We confirmed that the same expression pattern persists into the early postnatal period, although epicardial expression decreased noticeably from the middle of the first postnatal week and was essentially absent by postnatal day P7 (Figure 1A,B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by in situ hybridization data shown in figures.

claim: Epicardial Igf2 expression decreased noticeably from the middle of the first postnatal week and was essentially absent by postnatal day P7.
source: We confirmed that the same expression pattern persists into the early postnatal period, although epicardial expression decreased noticeably from the middle of the first postnatal week and was essentially absent by postnatal day P7 (Figure 1A,B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by in situ hybridization data shown in figures.

claim: Endocardial Igf2 expression at the RNA level was diminished quantitatively by P7, although was still clearly expressed.
source: Endocardial Igf2 expression at the RNA level was diminished quantitatively by P7, although was still clearly expressed.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by in situ hybridization data.

claim: Myocardial expression of Igf2 was not detected at any point during the early postnatal period.
source: At no point was myocardial expression of Igf2 detected.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by in situ hybridization data.

claim: Apical resection of the neonatal mouse heart at P1 is followed by robust cardiomyocyte proliferation and efficient regeneration.
source: Apical resection of the neonatal mouse heart at P1 is followed by robust cardiomyocyte proliferation and efficient regeneration (Porrello et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Apical resection did not affect Igf2 expression, spatially or quantitatively.
source: We noted that apical resection did not affect Igf2 expression, spatially or quantitatively (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by RT-PCR and in situ hybridization data shown in figures.

claim: The total amount of ventricular IGF2 protein was unchanged from birth through P7 and regardless of injury.
source: Interestingly, the total amount of ventricular IGF2 protein was unchanged from birth through P7 and regardless of injury (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), despite the loss of epicardial Igf2 expression and the diminished level of endocardial Igf2 expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by Western blot data shown in figures.

claim: The IGF2 protein present at P7 may have been translated several days earlier, and may be stabilized and/or sequestered by binding proteins.
source: The protein present at P7 may have been translated several days earlier, and may be stabilized and/or sequestered by binding proteins.
evidence: This is presented as a possible explanation for the observation.

claim: There is no apparent requirement for IGF2 protein in postnatal heart biology in the uninjured heart.
source: In the uninjured heart, there is no apparent requirement for this protein in postnatal heart biology, as genetic Igf2 manipulation with several Cre lines (Shen et al., 2015) had no recognizable postnatal consequence.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Nkx2.5-Cre drives efficient recombination in endocardium, epicardium, and myocardium because of its expression in early heart mesoderm lineage progenitors.
source: Because of its expression in early heart mesoderm lineage progenitors (van Wijk and van den Hoff, 2010), Nkx2.5-Cre drives efficient recombination in endocardium, epicardium, and myocardium, although at later stages, NKX2.5 protein is only expressed in cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: At later stages, NKX2.5 protein is only expressed in cardiomyocytes.
source: Because of its expression in early heart mesoderm lineage progenitors (van Wijk and van den Hoff, 2010), Nkx2.5-Cre drives efficient recombination in endocardium, epicardium, and myocardium, although at later stages, NKX2.5 protein is only expressed in cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Nkx2.5-Cre/Igf2 mutants have a hypoplastic ventricle phenotype and reduced cardiomyocyte proliferation during embryonic days E10-13.
source: As noted above, Nkx2.5-Cre/Igf2 mutants have a hypoplastic ventricle phenotype and reduced cardiomyocyte proliferation during embryonic days E10-13, although recover their level of cardiomyocyte proliferation at E14 and survive embryogenesis and have a normal adult lifespan.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior work cited earlier in the manuscript.

claim: Nkx2.5-Cre/Igf2 mutants recover their level of cardiomyocyte proliferation at E14 and survive embryogenesis and have a normal adult lifespan.
source: As noted above, Nkx2.5-Cre/Igf2 mutants have a hypoplastic ventricle phenotype and reduced cardiomyocyte proliferation during embryonic days E10-13, although recover their level of cardiomyocyte proliferation at E14 and survive embryogenesis and have a normal adult lifespan.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior work cited earlier in the manuscript.

claim: Other models with an early non-lethal cardiomyocyte deficiency have demonstrated extension of cardiomyocyte proliferation in late gestation to fully reconstitute the cardiomyocyte population by birth.
source: Other models with an early non-lethal cardiomyocyte deficiency have also demonstrated extension of cardiomyocyte proliferation in late gestation to fully reconstitute the cardiomyocyte population by birth (Drenckhahn et al., 2008; Vincentz et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nkx2.5-Cre/Igf2 mutants had normal heart morphology, heart size, and cardiomyocyte size both at birth and at P21.
source: We confirmed that Nkx2.5-Cre/Igf2 mutants had normal heart morphology, heart size, and cardiomyocyte size both at birth and at P21 (Figure 2A–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by histological and morphometric data shown in figures.

claim: At P3, control and Igf2 mutant hearts were comparable in both mononuclear cardiomyocyte percentage and mononuclear cardiomyocyte nuclear ploidy.
source: At P3, control and Igf2 mutant hearts were comparable in both mononuclear cardiomyocyte percentage and mononuclear cardiomyocyte nuclear ploidy, with calculated mononuclear diploid cardiomyocyte levels of 80.1 ± 6.4% (Cre only) and 85.1 ± 3.5% (Nkx2.5-Cre/Igf2).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by ploidy analysis data.

claim: By P7, the mononuclear diploid cardiomyocyte level had dropped dramatically in the hearts of both control and Igf2 mutant genotypes (to 14.7 ± 1.8% and 11.9 ± 1.1%, respectively).
source: By P7, this had dropped dramatically in the hearts of both genotypes (to 14.7 ± 1.8% and 11.9 ± 1.1%, respectively).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by ploidy analysis data.

claim: A slight difference at P7 in the mononuclear cardiomyocyte percentage between control and Igf2 mutants reached statistical significance.
source: We measured a slight difference at P7 in the mononuclear cardiomyocyte percentage that reached statistical significance, although we suspect this to be more likely explained by incidental factors (e.g., the number of pups per litter and the exact ages of each litter; pups from several litters were combined for this analysis).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by ploidy analysis data, but the authors express uncertainty about its biological significance.

claim: Nkx2.5-Cre/Igf2 mutants without injury are normal in postnatal heart biology.
source: Collectively, we conclude that Nkx2.5-Cre/Igf2 mutants without injury are normal in postnatal heart biology, with the uncertain possibility of a slight difference in mononuclear cardiomyocyte percentage at P7.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the study.

claim: Control mice predominantly had no scar or in a small number of cases had interspersed scar after P1 apex resection.
source: Control mice, all carrying either Nkx2.5-Cre or another Cre line described below but all wild-type for Igf2, predominantly had no scar or in a small number of cases had interspersed scar (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by histological data shown in figures and table.

claim: All Nkx2.5-Cre/Igf2 mutants had transmural scar after P1 apex resection.
source: In contrast, all Nkx2.5-Cre/Igf2 mutants had transmural scar (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by histological data shown in figures and table.

claim: Under typical experimental circumstances, IGF2 signaling is required for neonatal heart regeneration.
source: Thus, under these typical experimental circumstances, IGF2 signaling is required for neonatal heart regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the regeneration failure data in Igf2 mutants.

claim: The source of IGF2 required for neonatal heart regeneration is within rather than from outside the heart.
source: Furthermore, because of the cardiac mesoderm-restricted recombination domain of Nkx2.5-Cre, the source of IGF2 is within rather than from outside the heart.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic tools used in the study.

claim: The majority of resected neonates with Igf2 conditionally deleted in the endocardium and coronary endothelium completely (10/14) or partially (2/14) failed to regenerate.
source: Collectively, the majority of resected neonates with Igf2 conditionally deleted in the endocardium and coronary endothelium completely (10/14) or partially (2/14) failed to regenerate (Figure 3, Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by histological data shown in figures and table.

claim: The majority (6/8) of resected neonates with Igf2 conditionally deleted in the epicardium using Tbx18-Cre were fully restored 3 weeks later.
source: In contrast, the majority (6/8) of resected neonates with Igf2 conditionally deleted in the epicardium using Tbx18-Cre were fully restored 3 weeks later.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by histological data shown in table.

claim: The endocardium and coronary endothelium are the primary if not exclusive lineage source of IGF2 needed for neonatal heart regeneration.
source: These results strongly implicate the endocardium and coronary endothelium as the primary if not exclusive lineage source of IGF2 needed for neonatal heart regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lineage-specific Igf2 deletion data.

claim: The sole source of IGF2 in the embryonic heart that supports normal embryonic cardiomyocyte proliferation is the epicardium, with no apparent embryonic role for Igf2 expressed in the endocardial/endothelial lineage.
source: This is particularly surprising because the sole source of IGF2 in the embryonic heart that supports normal embryonic cardiomyocyte proliferation is the epicardium, with no apparent embryonic role whatsoever for Igf2 expressed in the endocardial/endothelial lineage (Shen et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: IGF2 can signal through the insulin receptor (INSR) and through the IGF1 receptor (IGF1R).
source: IGF2 can signal through the insulin receptor (INSR) and through the IGF1 receptor (IGF1R) (Scalia et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In the embryonic myocardium, only IGF1R is required to mediate IGF2 signaling, despite the seemingly comparable expression of the INSR.
source: In the embryonic myocardium, only IGF1R is required to mediate IGF2 signaling, despite the seemingly comparable expression of the INSR (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Only the insulin receptor is required for neonatal heart regeneration; there was little if any impact of Igf1r deficiency alone.
source: In testing the function of these receptors in neonatal heart regeneration, we unexpectedly found that only the insulin receptor is required; there was little if any impact of Igf1r deficiency alone (Table 1, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by histological data shown in table and figure.

claim: INSR function in cardiomyocytes mediates IGF2 response during neonatal heart regeneration.
source: The use of cardiomyocyte-specific Myh6-Cre in this analysis also demonstrates that INSR function in cardiomyocytes mediates IGF2 response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic tools used in the study.

claim: Phosphorylated INSR at 7dpr is eliminated when Igf2 is conditionally mutated.
source: Immunofluorescence detection of phosphorylated INSR at 7dpr is eliminated when Igf2 is conditionally mutated; there is no signal in the absence of injury (sham).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There is no detectable phosphorylation of IGF1R regardless of injury or Igf2 status in the 7dpr neonatal heart.
source: No detectable phosphorylation of IGF1R regardless of injury or Igf2 status in the 7dpr neonatal heart.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: At 3 and 7 days following sham surgery, there was no basal level of phosphorylation of either INSR or IGF1R.
source: By immunofluorescence using antibodies specific for phospho-INSR and for phospho-IGF1R, at 3 and 7 days following sham surgery, there was no basal level of phosphorylation of either receptor, indicating that the activity of the IGF/insulin signaling axis in the normal uninjured neonatal heart is below detection using this method (Figure 4B,C; Figure 4—figure supplements 1A and 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by immunofluorescence data shown in figures.

claim: The activity of the IGF/insulin signaling axis in the normal uninjured neonatal heart is below detection using immunofluorescence.
source: By immunofluorescence using antibodies specific for phospho-INSR and for phospho-IGF1R, at 3 and 7 days following sham surgery, there was no basal level of phosphorylation of either receptor, indicating that the activity of the IGF/insulin signaling axis in the normal uninjured neonatal heart is below detection using this method (Figure 4B,C; Figure 4—figure supplements 1A and 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunofluorescence data.

claim: IGF2 protein is present in the heart during the early postnatal period but seemingly in a manner that does not activate a substantial level of signaling.
source: IGF2 protein is present in the heart during this period (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), but seemingly in a manner that does not activate a substantial level of signaling (see below and Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference based on the Western blot and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Resection caused prominent INSR phosphorylation in a pattern that was somewhat heterogeneous even among nearby cardiomyocytes.
source: Resection caused prominent INSR phosphorylation (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplements 1A and 2), in a pattern that was somewhat heterogeneous even among nearby cardiomyocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B); the explanation for this heterogeneity is unknown.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by immunofluorescence data shown in figures.

claim: INSR phosphorylation was prominent in cardiomyocytes adjacent to the resection plane as well as distal to the injury.
source: INSR phosphorylation was prominent in cardiomyocytes adjacent to the resection plane as well as distal to the injury (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplements 1C and 2), which is consistent with the observation that cardiomyocyte proliferation is activated throughout the myocardium after neonatal injury (Porrello et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by immunofluorescence data shown in figures and consistent with prior work.

claim: INSR phosphorylation was eliminated in Nkx2.5-Cre/Igf2 conditional ligand mutants.
source: Importantly, INSR phosphorylation was eliminated in Nkx2.5-Cre/Igf2 conditional ligand mutants (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), confirming that IGF2 is the ligand that activates INSR during neonatal heart regeneration.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by immunofluorescence data shown in figures.

claim: IGF2 is the ligand that activates INSR during neonatal heart regeneration.
source: Importantly, INSR phosphorylation was eliminated in Nkx2.5-Cre/Igf2 conditional ligand mutants (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), confirming that IGF2 is the ligand that activates INSR during neonatal heart regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunofluorescence data in Igf2 mutants.

claim: IGF2 expression at the RNA and protein level is not changed by injury.
source: Because IGF2 expression at the RNA and protein level is not changed by injury (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), we assume that injury releases the block that prevents signaling in the uninjured heart.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by RT-PCR and Western blot data shown in figures.

claim: Injury releases the block that prevents IGF2 signaling in the uninjured heart.
source: Because IGF2 expression at the RNA and protein level is not changed by injury (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), we assume that injury releases the block that prevents signaling in the uninjured heart.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that IGF2 levels don't change but signaling is activated after injury.

claim: No IGF1R phosphorylation was observed in injured (or uninjured) neonatal hearts.
source: We observed no IGF1R phosphorylation in injured (or uninjured) neonatal hearts (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), which correlates with the absence of genetic requirement for this receptor in regeneration (Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by immunofluorescence data shown in figures.

claim: Absence of IGF1R phosphorylation in injured conditional Igf2 mutants demonstrates that IGF1 does not compensate for loss of IGF2.
source: Absence of IGF1R phosphorylation in injured conditional Igf2 mutants also demonstrates that IGF1 (which signals only through the IGF1R) does not compensate for loss of IGF2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunofluorescence data.

claim: IGF1R phosphorylation but no activation of the INSR was detected in embryonic heart.
source: As a positive control for reagent quality and specificity, we detected IGF1R phosphorylation but no activation of the INSR in embryonic heart (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), consistent with our previous observations (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by immunofluorescence data shown in figures and consistent with prior work.

claim: A very faint signal of phosphorylated receptor was detected in uninjured control heart tissue that was absent from conditional Insr mutants.
source: We detected a very faint signal of phosphorylated receptor in uninjured control heart tissue that was absent from conditional Insr mutants; this indicates a low basal level of INSR phosphorylation even though this was not detected by immunofluorescence (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Injury at P1 resulted in a prominent increase in phosphorylated receptor in 3dpr controls that was absent in Nkx2.5-Cre/Insr mutants.
source: Injury at P1 resulted in a prominent increase in phosphorylated receptor in 3dpr controls that was absent in Nkx2.5-Cre/Insr mutants.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: P1 heart injury selectively induces INSR phosphorylation but not IGF1R activation.
source: This analysis confirms that P1 heart injury selectively induces INSR phosphorylation but not IGF1R activation (even though IGF1R protein is present).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Western blot data.

claim: The insulin receptor gene is transcribed into two isoforms that differ only by the inclusion or exclusion of a 36 bp alternatively spliced exon 11.
source: The insulin receptor gene is transcribed into two isoforms that differ only by the inclusion or exclusion of a 36 bp alternatively spliced exon 11, resulting in proteins that differ by 12 amino acids in an extracellular domain of the receptor (Frasca et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The shorter form of INSR, called INSR-A, mediates signals by both insulin and IGF2, whereas the longer form, called INSR-B, responds to only insulin.
source: The shorter form, called INSR-A, mediates signals by both insulin and IGF2, whereas the longer form, called INSR-B, responds to only insulin (Frasca et al., 1999; Scalia et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Throughout the neonatal period, the ratio of the INSR A and B isoforms was roughly equal, and was not obviously altered after resection.
source: Throughout the neonatal period, the ratio of the A and B isoforms was roughly equal, and was not obviously altered after resection (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by RT-PCR data shown in figures.

claim: The insulin receptor A isoform that mediates IGF2 signals is present during the time when IGF2-INSR signaling is required for neonatal heart regeneration.
source: Thus, the insulin receptor A isoform that mediates IGF2 signals is present during the time when IGF2-INSR signaling is required for neonatal heart regeneration, and as demonstrated above is activated by IGF2 after neonatal heart injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RT-PCR and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Neonatal heart apex resection induces cardiomyocyte proliferation as a key element of the regenerative response.
source: Neonatal heart apex resection induces cardiomyocyte proliferation as a key element of the regenerative response (Porrello et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Three days after P1 sham surgery, a basal level of pH3+ staining was observed, reflecting the ongoing entry of cardiomyocytes into cell cycle that is followed in most cases by polyploidization.
source: Three days after P1 sham surgery, a basal level of pH3+ staining was observed, reflecting the ongoing entry of cardiomyocytes into cell cycle that is followed in most cases by polyploidization (Soonpaa et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by pH3 staining data and a citation to prior work.

claim: There was no difference in control vs. Igf2-deficient hearts in the uninjured 3dpr level of pH3+ cardiomyocytes.
source: There was no difference in control (Cre-only) vs. Igf2-deficient hearts in the uninjured 3dpr level of pH3+ cardiomyocytes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by pH3 staining data shown in figures.

claim: In genetically normal pups, P1 resection caused a substantial increase in the number of pH3+ cardiomyocytes at 3dpr.
source: In genetically normal pups, P1 resection caused a substantial increase in the number of pH3+ cardiomyocytes at 3dpr.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by pH3 staining data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The injury-induced increase in pH3+ cardiomyocytes at 3dpr was completely abrogated in conditional Igf2 mutants.
source: This response was completely abrogated in conditional Igf2 mutants (Figure 5B), indicating that IGF2 is required for this injury-induced mitogenic activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by pH3 staining data shown in figures.

claim: IGF2 is required for injury-induced mitogenic activity at 3dpr.
source: This response was completely abrogated in conditional Igf2 mutants (Figure 5B), indicating that IGF2 is required for this injury-induced mitogenic activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pH3 staining data.

claim: There is no indication of any additional activity at 3dpr that promotes pH3+ staining in a manner that is independent of IGF2.
source: There is no indication of any additional activity at 3dpr that promotes pH3+ staining, at least in a manner that is independent of IGF2 (Figure 5B').
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pH3 staining data.

claim: In genetic control mice, the level of pH3+ staining 7 days after sham surgery was several-fold lower than in sham-operated pups at 3dpr.
source: In genetic control mice (Cre-only), the level of pH3+ staining 7 days after sham surgery was several-fold lower than in sham-operated pups at 3dpr, as most cardiomyocytes have already undergone DNA replication and polyploidization by this time (Soonpaa et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by pH3 staining data and a citation to prior work.

claim: Absence of Igf2 did not change the basal level of pH3+ staining in sham-operated pups at 7dpr.
source: Absence of Igf2 did not change the basal level of pH3+ staining in sham-operated pups at 7dpr (Figure 5C), just as at 3dpr.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by pH3 staining data shown in figures.

claim: Injury at P1 resulted in robust cardiomyocyte pH3+ labeling that was still evident in control neonates at 7dpr.
source: Injury at P1 resulted in robust cardiomyocyte pH3+ labeling that was still evident in control neonates at 7dpr, just as at 3dpr.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by pH3 staining data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The percentage of pH3+ cardiomyocytes at 7dpr was also elevated in conditional Igf2 mutants compared to sham-operated animals.
source: Importantly, though, the percentage of pH3+ cardiomyocytes at 7dpr was also elevated in conditional Igf2 mutants compared to sham-operated animals (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by pH3 staining data shown in figures.

claim: There is an IGF2-independent activity that induces cardiomyocyte cell cycle entry at 7dpr.
source: This indicates the presence of an IGF2-independent activity that induces cardiomyocyte cell cycle entry at 7dpr, whereas IGF2 is required for all of the injury-induced pH3+ labeling at 3dpr.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pH3 staining data.

claim: Approximately 60% of the injury-induced pH3+ labeling at 7dpr is IGF2-independent.
source: Approx. 60% of the injury-induced pH3+ labeling at 7dpr is IGF2-independent (red bar in Figure 5C'), and 40% attributable to IGF2 (green bar in Figure 5C').
evidence: This is a quantitative conclusion drawn from the pH3 staining data shown in figures.

claim: The IGF2-independent activity at 7dpr is not necessarily in response to alternative mitogenic factors, as cardiomyocyte-intrinsic responses might also initiate cell cycle entry at this time.
source: It should be noted that the IGF2-independent activity at 7dpr is not necessarily in response to alternative mitogenic factors, as cardiomyocyte-intrinsic responses (recognition of strain or pressure, etc.) might also initiate cell cycle entry at this time.
evidence: This is presented as a caveat to the interpretation of the data.

claim: Phospho-histone H3 is a marker of cells in early mitosis, and does not necessarily indicate that cytokinesis will ensue.
source: Phospho-histone H3 is a marker of cells in early mitosis, and does not necessarily indicate that cytokinesis will ensue.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the pH3 marker.

claim: Injury in the adult heart induces cell cycle entry, including S-phase DNA replication and induction of pH3+ staining, but followed mostly by a failure to complete cytokinesis, resulting in cardiomyocytes with increased ploidy rather than an increased number of cardiomyocytes.
source: It is well established that injury in the adult heart induces cell cycle entry, including S-phase DNA replication and induction of pH3+ staining, but followed mostly by a failure to complete cytokinesis, resulting in cardiomyocytes with increased ploidy rather than an increased number of cardiomyocytes (Zebrowski et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Injury at P7 in wild-type pups is not followed by enough proliferation to support myocardial restoration.
source: For the same reason, injury at P7 in wild-type pups is not followed by enough proliferation to support myocardial restoration, as observed in previous studies (Porrello et al., 2011; Puente et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neonatal heart regeneration requires cardiomyocyte proliferation.
source: Our data support an interpretation that neonatal heart regeneration requires cardiomyocyte proliferation, that proliferation occurs during the first few days after P1 resection when a high percentage of cardiomyocytes are still able to divide, and that IGF2 acting as a typical mitogen is required during these first few days to induce cell cycle entry that then culminates in proliferation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented in the study.

claim: Proliferation occurs during the first few days after P1 resection when a high percentage of cardiomyocytes are still able to divide.
source: Our data support an interpretation that neonatal heart regeneration requires cardiomyocyte proliferation, that proliferation occurs during the first few days after P1 resection when a high percentage of cardiomyocytes are still able to divide, and that IGF2 acting as a typical mitogen is required during these first few days to induce cell cycle entry that then culminates in proliferation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented in the study.

claim: IGF2 acting as a typical mitogen is required during the first few days after P1 resection to induce cell cycle entry that then culminates in proliferation.
source: Our data support an interpretation that neonatal heart regeneration requires cardiomyocyte proliferation, that proliferation occurs during the first few days after P1 resection when a high percentage of cardiomyocytes are still able to divide, and that IGF2 acting as a typical mitogen is required during these first few days to induce cell cycle entry that then culminates in proliferation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented in the study.

claim: Even though there is abundant cell cycle activity at 7dpr, this is not followed by enough cytokinesis (proliferation) to support myocardial restoration.
source: In contrast, even though there is abundant cell cycle activity (e.g., pH3+ staining) at later times (e.g., at 7dpr), this is not followed by enough cytokinesis (proliferation) to support myocardial restoration.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented in the study.

claim: The main outcome of cell cycle activity at P7 is to increase the ploidy level of preexisting cardiomyocytes, rather than to increase the number of cardiomyocytes by proliferation.
source: Presumably, the main outcome of cell cycle activity at P7 is to increase the ploidy level of preexisting cardiomyocytes, rather than to increase the number of cardiomyocytes by proliferation.
evidence: This is presented as a presumption based on the data and prior knowledge.

claim: Several experimental manipulations that lower the level of reactive oxygen were previously shown to prolong the postnatal window during which cardiomyocytes remain proliferative.
source: Several experimental manipulations that lower the level of reactive oxygen were previously shown to prolong the postnatal window during which cardiomyocytes remain proliferative (Puente et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Raising newborn pups in a mildly hypoxic environment (15% oxygen) prolongs the postnatal window during which cardiomyocytes remain proliferative.
source: One method was to raise newborn pups in a mildly hypoxic environment (15% oxygen).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: Regeneration in genetic control mice was unaffected by mild hypoxia (i.e., occurred effectively).
source: Regeneration in genetic control mice (n = 9) was unaffected by mild hypoxia (i.e., occurred effectively), just as under normoxic conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Mild hypoxia was sufficient to rescue heart regeneration in Nkx2.5-Cre/Igf2 mutants: 4/5 displayed no scar and 1/5 displayed interspersed scar 21 days after resection.
source: Impressively, as evaluated by histology, mild hypoxia was sufficient to rescue heart regeneration in Nkx2.5-Cre/Igf2 mutants: 4/5 displayed no scar and 1/5 displayed interspersed scar 21 days after resection (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by histological data shown in figures.

claim: Transgenic expression of catalase directed to mitochondria (mCAT) lowers oxidative stress.
source: Transgenic expression of catalase directed to mitochondria (mCAT) lowers oxidative stress, and like mild hypoxia was previously shown to prolong cardiomyocyte proliferation (Puente et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The mCAT transgene combined with conditional Nfatc1-Cre/Igf2 mutation under normoxic conditions resulted in complete regeneration in 3 of 3 pups after P1 injury.
source: Here, we combined the mCAT transgene with conditional Nfatc1-Cre/Igf2 mutation under normoxic conditions, and after P1 injury observed complete regeneration in 3 of 3 pups (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by histological data shown in figures.

claim: Rescue of heart regeneration after P1 injury in Igf2 mutant neonates by mild hypoxia and by expression of the mCAT transgene minimizes the likelihood of an explanation for either other than through their common established mechanism to lower oxidative stress and thereby delay the postnatal onset of cardiomyocyte cell cycle arrest.
source: Rescue of heart regeneration after P1 injury in Igf2 mutant neonates by mild hypoxia and by expression of the mCAT transgene minimizes the likelihood of an explanation for either other than through their common established mechanism to lower oxidative stress and thereby delay the postnatal onset of cardiomyocyte cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the rescue data.

claim: One explanation for rescue of regeneration in Igf2 mutants by mild hypoxia and mCAT is a more effective proliferative response to the later mitogenic activity that is present around P7 even in mutants.
source: Since the early (P3) IGF2-dependent mitogenic activity is absent in Igf2 mutants (Figure 5B), one explanation for rescue of regeneration is a more effective proliferative response to the later mitogenic activity that is present around P7 even in mutants (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is presented as a possible explanation for the rescue data.

claim: In mice, almost all ventricular cardiomyocytes transition from mononuclear diploid to multinuclear and/or polyploid during the first postnatal week; a small percentage persist as mononuclear and diploid.
source: In mice, almost all ventricular cardiomyocytes transition from mononuclear diploid to multinuclear and/or polyploid during the first postnatal week; a small percentage persist as mononuclear and diploid.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cardiomyocyte ploidy.

claim: The transition from mononuclear diploid to multinuclear and/or polyploid occurs concurrent with the loss of efficient regenerative ability.
source: This transition occurs concurrent with the loss of efficient regenerative ability (Soonpaa et al., 1996; Alkass et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Recent experimental evidence demonstrates that mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes are proliferative and regenerative in adult mouse and zebrafish.
source: Recent experimental evidence demonstrates that mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes are proliferative and regenerative in adult mouse and zebrafish (Patterson et al., 2017; González-Rosa et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ubiquitous expression of the mCAT transgene elevates the percentage of mononuclear cardiomyocytes and of mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes in the adult mouse heart, with no effect on nuclear ploidy.
source: We recently reported that ubiquitous expression of the mCAT transgene elevates the percentage of mononuclear cardiomyocytes and of mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes in the adult mouse heart, with no effect on nuclear ploidy (Gan et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Measurements in the uninjured adult heart reflect the interruption or completion of mitosis during the first postnatal week, as there is so little cell cycle activity thereafter.
source: Measurements in the uninjured adult heart reflect the interruption or completion of mitosis during the first postnatal week, as there is so little cell cycle activity thereafter.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of adult heart measurements.

claim: mCAT expression resulted in a 2-fold increase in mononuclear cardiomyocyte level at P7.
source: We confirmed that mCAT expression resulted in a 2-fold increase in mononuclear cardiomyocyte level at P7 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) as also seen in the adult.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by ploidy analysis data shown in figures.

claim: Strain A/J mice have a particularly high level of mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes in the adult heart.
source: In our recent analysis (Patterson et al., 2017), we demonstrated that strain A/J mice have a particularly high level of mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes in the adult heart.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Both A/J and C57BL/6J strains reached their final adult mononuclear cardiomyocyte level shortly after P7, with that of A/J mice being 3-fold higher than that of C57BL/6J mice.
source: Both strains reached their final adult level shortly after P7, with that of A/J mice being 3-fold higher than that of C57BL/6J mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by ploidy analysis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The process of inducing polyploidy is primarily manifest during the first postnatal week, with genetic differences between strains responsible for determining the percentage of cardiomyocytes that become polyploid or remain mononuclear and diploid.
source: This is consistent with an understanding that the process of inducing polyploidy is primarily manifest during the first postnatal week, with genetic differences between strains responsible for determining the percentage of cardiomyocytes that become polyploid or remain mononuclear and diploid (Patterson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation consistent with the data and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: IGF2 is not relevant to the process of determining the percentage of cardiomyocytes that become polyploid or remain mononuclear and diploid.
source: IGF2 is not relevant to this process, as absence of Igf2 did not change the percentage of mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes at P3 and at most only minimally at P7 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ploidy analysis data in Igf2 mutants.

claim: All of 3 Nkx2.5-Cre/Igf2 pups on the A/J background had regenerated after P1 apex resection.
source: Importantly, all of 3 Nkx2.5-Cre/Igf2 pups had also regenerated (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by histological data shown in figures.

claim: When the number of mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes at P7 is elevated by strain background, the mitogenic activity present around that time is able to drive a sufficient degree of cardiomyocyte response to accomplish heart regeneration even in P1-injured Igf2 mutants.
source: Thus, even without environmental or transgenic manipulation, when the number of mononuclear diploid cardiomyocytes at P7 is elevated (e.g., here by strain background), the mitogenic (cell cycle entry) activity present around that time (Figure 5C) is able to drive a sufficient degree of cardiomyocyte response to accomplish heart regeneration even in P1-injured Igf2 mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the A/J strain rescue data.

claim: In the uninjured adult heart, Igf2 expression was not detectable by in situ hybridization, and was barely detectable by RT-PCR.
source: In the uninjured adult heart, Igf2 expression was not detectable by in situ hybridization, and was barely detectable by RT-PCR (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by in situ hybridization and RT-PCR data shown in figures.

claim: After adult heart injury (permanent coronary artery ligation), Igf2 expression was reexpressed in the endocardium in the infarcted zone, strongly at 6 days and continuing although to a declining level at 20 days.
source: After adult heart injury (permanent coronary artery ligation), we observed that Igf2 expression was reexpressed in the endocardium in the infarcted zone, strongly at 6 days and continuing although to a declining level at 20 days.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Igf2 reexpression after adult heart injury was not associated with INSR phosphorylation (activation).
source: This was however not associated with INSR phosphorylation (activation) (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by immunofluorescence data shown in figures.

claim: The situation after adult heart injury resembles the situation in the uninjured neonatal heart, where Igf2 is expressed and the protein is present but does not induce receptor activation, and where cardiomyocyte proliferation is minimal.
source: This resembles the situation in the uninjured neonatal heart, where Igf2 is expressed and the protein is present but does not induce receptor activation, and where cardiomyocyte proliferation is minimal.
evidence: This is a comparison drawn between adult and neonatal heart observations.

claim: Under normal circumstances, the window of heart regenerative competence in mice is limited to only the first few days of the first postnatal week.
source: First, our studies support the view that under normal circumstances, the window of heart regenerative competence in mice is limited to only the first few days of the first postnatal week.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: A similar temporal conclusion about the window of heart regenerative competence was reached by others.
source: A similar temporal conclusion was reached by others (Ikenishi et al., 2012; Notari et al., 2018), and is a further refinement of the observation that heart injury at P7 is not followed by effective regeneration (Porrello et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Igf2 deficiency unmasks early and late first week cell cycle entry activity and distinguishes the necessity of the former for functional tissue regeneration.
source: Igf2 deficiency therefore unmasks early and late first week cell cycle entry activity and distinguishes the necessity of the former for functional tissue regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: IGF2 appears to be the prime if not sole mitogenic factor that directly induces neonatal cardiomyocyte proliferation during the first few days after P1 injury.
source: Second, IGF2 appears to be the prime if not sole mitogenic factor that directly induces neonatal cardiomyocyte proliferation during the first few days after P1 injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: In Igf2 mutants there was no indication of any further activity that even partially contributes to an increase in cell cycle entry after P1 injury at 3dpr.
source: In Igf2 mutants there was no indication of any further activity that even partially contributes to an increase in cell cycle entry after P1 injury (Figure 5B').
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pH3 staining data.

claim: Effective regeneration does not occur in Igf2 mutants despite robust cell cycle activity at 7dpr.
source: For this reason, effective regeneration does not occur in Igf2 mutants despite robust cell cycle activity at 7dpr.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Other secreted factors previously studied in the context of neonatal heart regeneration may indirectly influence cardiomyocyte proliferation through alternative cell types or mechanisms.
source: Other secreted factors previously studied in the context of neonatal heart regeneration (Kawagishi et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2018; Das et al., 2019; Wodsedalek et al., 2019) may indirectly influence cardiomyocyte proliferation through alternative cell types or mechanisms, although we cannot formally exclude the possibility that IGF2 and another secreted mitogen are required together to induce proliferation.
evidence: This is presented as a possible explanation for the role of other factors, with citations to prior work.

claim: It is notable that neonatal heart regeneration relies on paracrine signaling.
source: Third, it is notable that neonatal heart regeneration relies on paracrine signaling at all.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Changes in cardiac output or wall strain after injury might be detected directly by cardiomyocytes, either at myocyte-myocyte junctions or at the cell surface via interaction with extracellular matrix.
source: In principle, changes in cardiac output or wall strain after injury might be detected directly by cardiomyocytes, either at myocyte-myocyte junctions or at the cell surface via interaction with extracellular matrix.
evidence: This is presented as a theoretical possibility.

claim: Such processes (direct detection of changes by cardiomyocytes) and others are clearly relevant but do not substitute for the requirement for IGF2-INSR paracrine signaling.
source: Such processes (Bassat et al., 2017; Notari et al., 2018) and others (Mahmoud et al., 2015) are clearly relevant but do not substitute for the requirement for IGF2-INSR paracrine signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Conditional manipulation of Igf2 in cardiac endothelium and cardiomyocyte-specific manipulation of Insr establish IGF2 signaling through INSR as the major paracrine pathway that underlies neonatal heart regeneration.
source: Our conditional manipulation of Igf2 in cardiac endothelium and cardiomyocyte-specific manipulation of Insr establish IGF2 signaling through INSR as the major paracrine pathway that underlies this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Certain circumstances can override the requirement for IGF2 signaling in neonatal regeneration.
source: Fourth, certain circumstances can override the requirement for IGF2 signaling in neonatal regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Mild hypoxia, mCAT expression, and an inbred A/J strain background were each individually sufficient to support efficient regeneration in the absence of IGF2.
source: In this study, we found that mild hypoxia, mCAT expression, and an inbred A/J strain background were each individually sufficient to support efficient regeneration in the absence of IGF2.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: The rescue of regeneration in Igf2 mutants by mild hypoxia, mCAT, and A/J strain reflects a higher frequency of completed cell cycle events (i.e., proliferation) among the cardiomyocytes that are induced by P1 injury to enter cell cycle during the later part of the first week.
source: We interpret these outcomes (see model in Figure 8) to reflect a higher frequency of completed cell cycle events (i.e., proliferation) among the cardiomyocytes that are induced by P1 injury to enter cell cycle during the later part of the first week, when factors other than IGF2 are present (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the rescue data.

claim: A limitation of the analysis is that proliferation was not directly measured, which for cardiomyocytes is recognized as very difficult to distinguish from polyploidization.
source: We note a limitation of our analysis is that we have not directly measured proliferation, which for cardiomyocytes is recognized as very difficult to distinguish from polyploidization (Soonpaa et al., 2013; Zebrowski et al., 2016; Leone et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Because cardiomyocyte proliferation is necessary for heart regeneration, rescue of regeneration in Igf2 mutants must have involved proliferation.
source: Because cardiomyocyte proliferation is necessary for heart regeneration, we infer that rescue of regeneration in Igf2 mutants must have involved proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the necessity of proliferation for regeneration.

claim: The observations serve as a caution in interpretation of results when strain background or environment are not properly controlled.
source: Our observations also serve as a caution in interpretation of results when strain background or environment are not properly controlled.
